title: Optimal Algorithms for Bounded Weighted Edit Distance
authors: Alejandro Cassis (Saarland University and Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus, Germany), Tomasz Kociumaka (Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus, Germany), Philip Wellnitz (Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus, Germany)
abstract: The edit distance (also known as Levenshtein distance) of two strings is the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions of characters needed to transform one string into the other. The textbook dynamic-programming algorithm computes the edit distance of two length-n strings in O(n^2) time, which is optimal up to subpolynomial factors and conditioned on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH). An established way of circumventing this hardness is to consider the bounded setting, where the running time is parameterized by the edit distance k. A celebrated algorithm by Landau and Vishkin (JCSS’88) achieves a running time of O(n + k^2), which is optimal as a function of n and k (again, up to subpolynmial factors and conditioned on SETH). While the theory community thoroughly studied the Levenshtein distance, most practical applications rely on a more general weighted edit distance, where each edit has a weight depending on its type and the involved characters from the alphabet Σ. This is formalized through a weight function w : Σ∪{ε}×Σ∪{ε} → R normalized so that w(a ↦ a) = 0 for a ∈ Σ ∪ {ε} and w(a ↦ b) ≥ 1 for a, b ∈ Σ ∪ {ε} with a ̸= b; the goal is to find an alignment of the two strings minimizing the total weight of edits. The classic O(n^2)-time algorithm supports this setting seamlessly, but for many decades just a straightforward O(nk)-time solution was known for the bounded version of the weighted edit distance problem. Only very recently, Das, Gilbert, Hajiaghayi, Kociumaka, and Saha (STOC’23) gave the first nontrivial algorithm, achieving a time complexity of O(n+k^5). While this running time is linear for k ≤ n^{1/5}, it is still very far from O(n+k^2)—the bound achievable in the unweighted setting. This is unsatisfactory, especially given the lack of any compelling evidence that the weighted version is inherently harder. In this paper, we essentially close this gap by showing both an improved tilde-O(n + √(nk^3))-time algorithm and, more surprisingly, a matching lower bound: Conditioned on the All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) hypothesis, the running time of our solution is optimal for √n ≤ k ≤ n (up to subpolynomial factors). In particular, this is the first separation between the complexity of the weighted and unweighted edit distance problems. Just like the Landau–Vishkin algorithm, our algorithm can be adapted to a wide variety of settings, such as when the input is given in a compressed representation. This is because, independently of the string length n, our procedure takes tilde-O(k^3) time assuming that the equality of any two substrings can be tested in tilde-O(1) time. Consistently with the previous work, our algorithm relies on the observation that strings with a rich structure of lowweight alignments must contain highly repetitive substrings. Nevertheless, achieving the optimal running time requires multiple new insights. We capture the right notion of repetitiveness using a tailor-made compressibility measure that we call selfedit distance. Our divide-and-conquer algorithm reduces the computation of weighted edit distance to several subproblems involving substrings of small self-edit distance and, at the same time, distributes the budget for edit weights among these subproblems. We then exploit the repetitive structure of the underlying substrings using state-of-the-art results for multiplesource shortest paths in planar graphs (Klein, SODA’05). As a stepping stone for our conditional lower bound, we study a dynamic problem of maintaining two strings subject to updates (substitutions of characters) and weighted edit distance queries. We significantly extend the construction of Abboud and Dahlgaard (FOCS’16), originally for dynamic shortest paths in planar graphs, to show that a sequence of n updates and q ≤ n queries cannot be handled much faster than in O(n^2√q) time. We then compose the snapshots of the dynamic strings to derive hardness of the static problem in the bounded setting.

I. I NTRODUCTION
The edit distance (also known as the Levenshtein distance [1]) of two strings is the minimum number of insertions,
deletions, and substitutions of characters needed to transform
one string into the other. Computational problems that involve
edit distance have been extensively investigated for decades.
The textbook dynamic-programming algorithm [2]–[5] computes the edit distance between two strings of lengths at most n
in time O(n2 ). This is optimal up to subpolynomial factors under the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis (OVH) [6]–[9], which,
in turn, follows from the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [10], [11]. An established way to circumvent this
hardness is to study the bounded setting, where we measure the
running time both by the length n of the input strings and by
their edit distance k. For this setting, the celebrated algorithm
of Landau and Vishkin [12], building upon earlier results of
Ukkonen [13] and Myers [14], runs in time O(n + k 2 ), which

many recent advancements in approximation and sublineartime algorithms for edit distance [15], [16], and its running
time is optimal as a function of n and k (again up to
subpolynomial factors under OVH); see for instance [17].
While the theoretical computer science community has
extensively studied the Levenshtein distance, most real-world
applications require the more general weighted edit distance,
where each edit is associated with a weight depending
on its type and the involved characters from the alphabet
Σ [18]–[21]; see also [22, Section 11.5.2] for a discussion
of weight functions used in bioinformatics. Consequently, the
weighted edit distance has been studied since the earliest
papers concerned with edit distance [4], [5], [18], [23]. The
weighted edit distance is formalized through a weight function
w : Σ ∪ {ε} × Σ ∪ {ε} → R, which can be normalized so that
w(a → a) = 0 for a ∈ Σ ∪ {ε} and w(a → b) ≥ 1 for
a, b ∈ Σ ∪ {ε} with a = b. The underlying problem asks to
align the two input strings while minimizing the total weight
of the edits performed. The standard dynamic-programming
O(n2 )-time algorithm supports this setting seamlessly, but for
many decades just a straightforward O(nk)-time solution was
known for the bounded variant of weighted edit distance.
In particular, the algorithm by Landau and Vishkin does
not extend to the weighted case. Perhaps surprisingly, only
recently Das, Gilbert, Hajiaghayi, Kociumaka, and Saha [24]
obtained the ﬁrst O(n + poly(k))-time algorithm for weighted
edit distance. More precisely, their deterministic algorithm
runs in time O(n + k 5 )—leaving open a wide gap between
the unweighted and weighted settings. In particular, the most
fundamental separation question remained unsettled:

B. Related Work
Edit distance has been studied extensively since the
1960s [1]–[3], [5], [27], with the history of the bounded
version reaching mid-1980s [12]–[14]. The quadratic hardness
result conditioned on OVH [6]–[9] naturally motivates the
study of subquadratic approximation algorithms [28]–[34].
The current best approximation algorithm in almost linear time
is due to Andoni and Nosatzki [35], achieving a constantfactor approximation in time O(n1+δ ) for any constant δ > 0.
Sublinear-time approximations have also ﬂourished in the
last few years [15], [16], [29], [36]–[38]. None of these
approximation algorithms extend to weighted edit distance,
where the current state of the art, due to Kuszmaul [39], is an
O(nδ )-approximation in time O(n2−δ ) for any 0 ≤ δ ≤ 1.
The (unweighted) bounded edit distance problem has also
been studied in multiple other settings: there are efﬁcient
sketching & streaming algorithms [40]–[43], algorithms for
compressed strings [44], and algorithms for preprocessed
data [33], [45]. Recent works have also focused on the
bounded version of two related problems: Dyck edit distance [46]–[48] and tree edit distance [49], [50]. The O(n +
poly(k))-time weighted-edit-distance algorithm of [24] generalizes to these two settings (with mild additional assumptions
on the weight function, such as the triangle inequality), but the
dependency on k degrades to O(k12 ) and O(k 15 ) respectively.
Most of the earlier theoretical results for weighted edit
distance are limited to uniform weight functions that assign

In this section, we give a high-level overview of our results.
A. Improved Algorithms for Bounded Weighted Edit Distance
Let us start by brieﬂy reviewing the existing algorithms.
First, recall the textbook dynamic-programming algorithm for
edit distance that runs in quadratic time and, in particular, its
natural extension to the weighted edit distance. It is instructive
to view said algorithm in terms of the alignment graph of
the input strings X, Y , and the normalized weight function w
(consult the full version for a formal deﬁnition). The alignment
graph is a directed acyclic graph formed by a grid on the
vertices [ 0 . . |X| ]×[ 0 . . |Y | ] that is augmented with diagonal
edges.
For an intuition, visualize the vertex (0, 0) in the top left
corner of the grid and a vertex (x, y) in the x-th column and
y-th row of the grid. Now, we interpret
• a horizontal edge (x, y) → (x + 1, y) as a deletion
of X[ x ] and, accordingly, assign to it a weight of
w(X[ x ] → ε);
• a vertical edge (x, y) → (x, y+1) as an insertion of Y [ y ]
and, accordingly, assign to it a weight of w(ε → Y [ y ]);
• a diagonal edge (x, y) → (x + 1, y + 1) as a match or a
substitution of X[ x ] for Y [ y ] and, accordingly, assign
to it a weight of w(X[ x ] → Y [ y ]).
A diagonal in the alignment graph is a path that starts at some
vertex (x, 0) or (0, y) and proceeds along diagonal edges as
long as possible. The diagonal starting at (0, 0) is the main
diagonal.
Observe that the weighted edit distance between X and
Y corresponds to distance from (0, 0) to (|X|, |Y |) in the
alignment graph. Since the graph is acyclic, we can compute
this distance in time proportional to the graph size, which is

function, the weight of every horizontal and vertical edge in
the alignment graph is at least 1. Hence, all vertices (x, y) that
are at a distance of at most k from (0, 0) satisfy |x − y| ≤ k.
